facts.title: An Ancient Eye-Catcher
facts.text: Antimony has been used by humans for thousands of years, long before it was recognized as an element. Its black sulfide mineral, stibnite, was ground into the cosmetic kohl that ancient Egyptians and Mesopotamians used to darken their eyelids. A surviving Sumerian vase fragment thought to be partly antimony shows just how far back our relationship with this metalloid stretches.

facts.title: Why The Symbol Is Sb
facts.text: Antimony's chemical symbol, Sb, comes from its Latin name stibium, the word the Romans used for the eye-paint mineral stibnite. The English word 'antimony' itself likely derives from the medieval Latin antimonium used by alchemists. This split between modern name and ancient symbol is the same reason iron is Fe (ferrum) and sodium is Na (natrium).

facts.title: A Metal That Expands When It Freezes
facts.text: Most substances shrink as they solidify, but antimony is one of the rare exceptions that expands slightly when it freezes, behaving a bit like water turning to ice. This unusual property made it invaluable in old movable type: antimony-lead-tin alloys filled the tiny crevices of letter molds completely, producing crisp, sharp printed characters. Bismuth and gallium share this expand-on-freezing quirk.

facts.title: Metalloid On The Fence
facts.text: Antimony sits in group 15 of the periodic table and is classified as a metalloid, meaning it straddles the line between metals and nonmetals. The familiar silvery form is a brittle, shiny, crystalline solid that looks metallic but conducts heat and electricity poorly compared with true metals. It also exists in less stable nonmetallic allotropes, including a yellow form and an unstable black form.

facts.title: The Flame Retardant Workhorse
facts.text: By far the largest modern use of antimony is as antimony trioxide, a flame retardant. When combined with halogenated compounds in plastics, textiles, and electronics casings, it dramatically slows the spread of fire by interfering with combustion in the gas phase. This single application accounts for a large share of global antimony demand, much of it tied to safety regulations.

facts.title: Powering Batteries, Old And New
facts.text: Antimony has long hardened the lead plates inside ordinary lead-acid car batteries, improving their strength and durability. More recently it has drawn attention for grid-scale energy storage: researchers including MIT's Donald Sadoway pioneered liquid-metal batteries that use molten antimony as one electrode. Such batteries could one day help store electricity from solar and wind farms.

facts.title: Mostly Made In China
facts.text: Antimony is considered a critical raw material because its supply is heavily concentrated geographically. China dominates world production, mining well over half of global output, with Russia, Tajikistan, and Myanmar among other significant sources. This concentration, combined with its military and electronics uses, is why many governments classify antimony as strategically important.

facts.title: A Brush With Stardust
facts.text: Antimony is a relatively rare element in the universe, making up only a tiny fraction of Earth's crust. Astronomers have detected it in stars, and in 2020 antimony was identified in the atmosphere of an ancient, metal-poor star, offering clues about how heavy elements were forged. Much of the antimony in the cosmos is thought to form through neutron-capture processes in dying stars.

facts.title: Medicine, Past And Present
facts.text: For centuries antimony compounds were used, often dangerously, as purgatives and remedies, with reusable antimony 'perpetual pills' passed down through families. Today, far more refined antimony-based drugs such as sodium stibogluconate remain frontline treatments for leishmaniasis, a parasitic disease spread by sandflies. This shows how a once-toxic folk remedy evolved into a carefully dosed modern medicine.

facts.title: Toxic Cousin Of Arsenic
facts.text: Chemically, antimony closely resembles arsenic, sitting just below it in the periodic table, and it shares some of arsenic's toxicity. The human body has no known biological need for antimony, and high exposure can irritate the lungs and harm the heart and digestive system. Because of this, its use in food-contact materials and toys is tightly regulated, and stibine gas (SbH3) is especially hazardous.
